“If there is a God and there is a future life, then there is truth, there is virtue; and man’s highest happiness consists in striving to attain them. One must live, one must love, one must believe,” Pierre was saying, “that we do not live only now on this patch of earth, but that we have lived and shall live eternally there, in the whole of it” (he pointed to the sky). Prince Andrei stood leaning on the railing of the ferry and, as he listened to Pierre, gazed, without taking his eyes from it, at the red reflection of the sun on the water, which was turning blue. Pierre fell silent. It was completely quiet. The ferry had long since reached the bank, and only the waves of the current struck the bottom of the ferry with a faint sound. It seemed to Prince Andrei that this lapping of the waves added a refrain to Pierre’s words: “It is true; believe it.”

Prince Andrei sighed and looked with a radiant, childlike, tender gaze into Pierre’s flushed, ecstatic, yet still timid face—the face of a friend who held the leading place.

“Yes, if only it were so!” he said. “But let us go and sit down,” Prince Andrei added, and as he left the ferry, he looked at the sky to which Pierre had pointed, and for the first time since Austerlitz he saw that lofty, eternal sky which he had seen while lying on the field at Austerlitz; and something long dormant, something better that was within him, suddenly awoke joyfully and youthfully in his soul. This feeling vanished as soon as Prince Andrei once more entered the customary conditions of life, but he knew that this feeling, which he did not know how to develop, lived within him. His meeting with Pierre marked an epoch for Prince Andrei from which began a new life for him—outwardly the same as before, but new in his inner world.

XIII.

It was already growing dark when Prince Andrei and Pierre drove up to the main entrance of the house at Bald Hills. As they approached, Prince Andrei smilingly drew Pierre’s attention to the commotion that had arisen by the back porch. A bent old woman with a bundle on her back and a short man in a black garment, with long hair, saw the carriage driving in and rushed back toward the gate. Two women ran out after them, and all four, glancing back at the carriage, ran in fright onto the back porch.

“Those are Masha’s people of God,” said Prince Andrei. “They mistook us for Father. And this is the one thing in which she disobeys him: he orders these wanderers to be driven away, while she receives them.”

“But what are people of God?” Pierre asked.

Prince Andrei had no time to answer him. The servants came out to meet them, and he questioned them about where the old prince was and whether he was expected soon.

The old prince was still in town, and they expected him at any moment.

Prince Andrei took Pierre to his own suite of rooms, which was always kept in perfect order awaiting him in his father’s house, and went himself to the nursery.

“Let us go to my sister,” Prince Andrei said when he returned to Pierre. “I have not seen her yet; she is hiding now and sitting with her people of God. It serves her right: she will be embarrassed, and you will see the people of God. It is curious, upon my word.”

“What are people of God?” Pierre asked.

“You shall see.”

Princess Marya was indeed embarrassed and flushed in patches when they entered her room. In her cozy room, with icon lamps before the icon cases, a young boy with a long nose and long hair, wearing a monk’s cassock, sat beside her on the sofa behind the samovar.

Nearby, in an armchair, sat a wrinkled, thin old woman with a meek expression on her childlike face.

“André, why did you not warn me?” she said with gentle reproach, placing herself before her wanderers like a mother hen before her chicks.

“Delighted to see you. I am very glad to see you,” she said to Pierre as he kissed her hand. She had known him as a child, and now his friendship with Andrei, his friendship with Andrei’s wife, and, above all, his kind, simple face disposed her favorably toward him. She looked at him with her beautiful, radiant eyes and seemed to say, “I love you very much, but please do not laugh at my people.” After exchanging their first words of greeting, they sat down.

“Ah, so Ivanushka is here too,” said Prince Andrei, pointing with a smile to the young wanderer.

“André!” Princess Marya said imploringly.

“You must know that she is a woman,” Andrei said to Pierre.

“André, in God’s name!” Princess Marya repeated.

It was evident that Prince Andrei’s mocking attitude toward the wanderers and Princess Marya’s futile defense of them were customary, established relations between them.

“But, my dear friend,” said Prince Andrei, “you ought, on the contrary, to be grateful to me for explaining to Pierre your intimacy with this young man.”

“Really?” Pierre said curiously and seriously—which made Princess Marya particularly grateful to him—peering through his spectacles into the face of Ivanushka, who, realizing that they were speaking about him, looked around at everyone with sly eyes.

Princess Marya was embarrassed for her people quite needlessly. They were not at all timid. The old woman, with her eyes lowered but glancing sidelong at those who had entered, had turned her cup upside down on its saucer and placed a bitten piece of sugar beside it; she sat calmly and motionlessly in her armchair, waiting to be offered more tea. Ivanushka, sipping from his saucer, looked at the young men from under his brows with sly, feminine eyes.

“Where were you—in Kiev?” Prince Andrei asked the old woman.

“I was, Father,” the talkative old woman replied. “At Christmas itself I was vouchsafed, at the saints’ shrines, to partake of the holy, heavenly mysteries. And now I come from Kolyazin, Father; a great grace has been revealed there...”

“And is Ivanushka with you?”

“I travel on my own, provider,” Ivanushka said, trying to speak in a bass voice. “It was only in Yukhnov that Pelageyushka and I met...”

Pelageyushka interrupted her companion; she evidently wanted to tell what she had seen.

“In Kolyazin, Father, a great grace has been revealed.”

“What, some new relics?” Prince Andrei asked.

“That is enough, Andrei,” said Princess Marya. “Do not tell it, Pelageyushka.”

“No... what are you saying, Mother? Why should I not tell it? I love him. He is kind. He is chosen by God; he, my benefactor, gave me ten rubles—I remember. When I was in Kiev, Kiryusha, the holy fool—a true man of God, who goes barefoot winter and summer—says to me: ‘Why do you go where you ought not? Go to Kolyazin; a miracle-working icon has been revealed there, the most holy Mother of God.’ At those words I bade farewell to the saints and set out...”

Everyone was silent; the wanderer alone spoke in a measured voice, drawing in her breath.

“I arrived, my dear father, and the people say to me: ‘A great grace has been revealed; holy oil is dripping from the cheek of the most holy Mother of God...’”

“Very well, very well, you can tell it later,” Princess Marya said, blushing.

“Allow me to ask her,” said Pierre. “Did you see it yourself?” he asked.

“Of course, Father, I was vouchsafed to see it myself. There was such a radiance upon the countenance, like the light of heaven, and from the Mother’s cheek it kept dripping and dripping...”

“But that is a deception,” Pierre said ingenuously, having listened attentively to the wanderer.

“Oh, Father, what are you saying!” Pelageyushka said in horror, turning to Princess Marya for protection.

“They are deceiving the people,” he repeated.
